cards.front: Define and give the formula for the [[kw:mean]].
back: The arithmetic average of a set of numbers.
$$\text{Mean} = \frac{\text{Sum of all values}}{\text{Number of values}}$$
Sensitive to extreme values (outliers).
Number of values = 7.

cards.front: What is a [[kw:weighted mean]] and how is it calculated?
back: An average where each value is multiplied by its frequency (or weight) before summing.
$$\text{Weighted Mean} = \frac{\sum (x_i \times f_i)}{\sum f_i}$$
Used when some values occur more often or are more important.
Example: GPA is a weighted mean of grade points by credits.

cards.front: Calculate GPA: A (4 credits), B (3 credits), B (3 credits), C (2 credits).
back: Total credits = 4+3+3+2=12.
The middle value when data are ordered from smallest to largest.
Odd count: middle number; even count: average of the two middle numbers.
Not affected by outliers—better for skewed data (e.g., incomes, home prices).
cards.front: Define the [[kw:median]] and how to find it.
Find the median of: 27k, 32k, 40k, 67k, 95k.
back: Ordered: 27k, 32k, 40k, 67k, 95k.
5 values → 3rd is median = 40k.
The value that appears most frequently in a data set.
Can be one mode, multiple modes (bimodal), or no mode.
Best for categorical data or finding the most popular item (e.g., shoe size, color).
cards.front: Define the [[kw:mode]] and when it's most useful.

back: Mode = 10 (appears most often).
cards.front: Identify the mode(s) of: 5, 10, 15, 10, 20, 5, 10.
When should you use the median instead of the mean?
back: When the data has extreme values (outliers) that distort the mean.
Median gives a better picture of the 'typical' value in skewed distributions.
Example: median home price, median income.
A table that groups data into classes (intervals) and shows the count (frequency) in each class.
Steps: Find range (max–min), choose number of classes, compute class width (range/classes, round up), tally data.
Used to summarize large datasets and reveal patterns.
cards.front: What is a [[kw:frequency distribution]]?

back: Class width = 60 ÷ 6 = 10.
So intervals of size 10, e.g., 0-9, 10-19, …
cards.front: Calculate class width: data range = 60, desired classes = 6.

back: The fraction or percent of the total observations that fall into a class.
$$\text{Relative Frequency} = \frac{\text{Class Frequency}}{\text{Total Observations}} \times 100$$
Allows comparison across datasets of different sizes.
cards.front: What is [[kw:relative frequency]]?

back: Uses rectangular bars of equal width separated by spaces.
Categories on x‑axis, frequencies/values on y‑axis.
Best for comparing discrete categories at one point in time (e.g., sales by region).
[[imp:Vertical axis must start at zero to avoid misleading visuals.]]
cards.front: Describe a [[kw:bar graph]] and its appropriate use.
Explain a [[kw:line graph]] and when to use it.
back: Plots data points connected by lines, showing trends over time.
Time on x‑axis, variable on y‑axis.
Best for time‑series data (monthly sales, yearly profit).
Multiple lines can compare trends.
Divides a circle into slices proportional to category percentages of the whole.
$$\text{Slice Angle} = \text{Percent} \times 3.6°$$
Used to show parts‑of‑a‑whole (budget, market share).
[[imp:Total must equal 100%; limit slices for clarity.]]
cards.front: What is a [[kw:circle graph]] (pie chart) and how do you compute slice angles?
Calculate the slice angle for a category that is 35% of the total.

back: Compares the current price of an item to its price in a base period.
$$\text{Price Relative} = \frac{\text{Current Price}}{\text{Base Price}} \times 100$$
Above 100 = increase; below 100 = decrease.
cards.front: Define [[kw:price relative]] and its formula.

back: Prices increased 25% from the base period.
cards.front: Calculate price relative: base price \$4.00, current price \$5.00.
Define the [[kw:range]] in a dataset.
back: The difference between the maximum and minimum values.
$$\text{Range} = \text{Max} - \text{Min}$$
Simple but only uses two values; heavily influenced by outliers.

cards.front: What is the [[kw:standard deviation]] and how is it calculated for a sample?
back: Measures the average distance of data points from the mean.
$$s = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n-1}}$$
Larger SD = more variability; smaller SD = data clustered closer to mean.
Use n‑1 for samples to obtain an unbiased estimate.
Mean = 5.
Deviations: -3,-1,-1,-1,0,0,2,4; squares sum = 32.
cards.front: Compute sample standard deviation of: 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9.
Explain the [[kw:empirical rule]] (68‑95‑99.7 rule).
back: For normal (bell‑shaped) distributions:
~68% of data lie within ±1 SD of the mean.
~95% within ±2 SD.
~99.7% within ±3 SD.
Useful for detecting outliers and understanding data spread.
[[imp:Only valid for approximately normal distributions.]]

cards.front: A normal distribution has mean 200 and SD 25. What percentage of values are between 175 and 225?
back: By empirical rule: about 68%.

cards.front: What is the [[kw:coefficient of variation (CV)]]?
back: A relative measure of variability expressed as a percentage of the mean.
$$\text{CV} = \frac{\text{SD}}{\text{Mean}} \times 100$$
Unitless – ideal for comparing variability across datasets with different means or units.
Lower CV indicates greater consistency.
Fund A has higher CV → relatively riskier.
cards.front: Fund A: mean return 12%, SD 3%. Fund B: mean return 9%, SD 1.8%. Which is relatively riskier?

back: [[imp:Understand:]] data list, sample or population, required measures.
[[imp:Solve:]] compute mean, range, squared deviations, variance, SD, CV if needed.
[[imp:Conclude:]] interpret SD/CV in context; use empirical rule if distribution is normal.
cards.front: What is the blueprint for solving measures of dispersion problems?

back: Raw deviations sum to zero (positives cancel negatives).
Squaring removes negatives and emphasizes larger deviations.
This gives a true measure of overall spread.
cards.front: Why do we square deviations in standard deviation?
True or False: The standard deviation can be negative.
back: False. Standard deviation ≥ 0, zero only when all data are identical.
When comparing variability of datasets with different units (e.g., dollars vs. kilograms) or very different means.
CV normalizes the spread relative to the average.
cards.front: When is the coefficient of variation preferred over standard deviation?
Why should a bar graph's vertical axis start at zero?
back: Starting above zero can exaggerate differences between bars, misleading viewers.
Zero baseline ensures proportional representation of values.
Circle graph (pie chart).
Bar graphs and line graphs compare individual items or trends, not proportions of a total.
